title: Potassium‐Concentration‐Gated C–N Coupling Enables a Volcano‐Shaped Selectivity Window for Electrocatalytic Urea Synthesis
content:
Potassium concentration opens an optimal selectivity window for urea electrosynthesis on Cu. At an intermediate K+ concentration, favorable precursor geometry alignment and balanced electronic activation minimize the *CO–*NO coupling barrier and enhance urea selectivity. Molecular simulations and infrared spectroscopy link this response to changes in reaction energetics and the interfacial environment, guiding electrolyte design for selective urea formation.








ABSTRACT
Alkali metal cations influence electrochemical interfaces, but their role in regulating urea electrosynthesis remains incompletely understood. Here, we combine constant‐potential ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), classical molecular dynamics (cMD), flow‐cell electrolysis, and in situ infrared spectroscopy to investigate how cations affect urea formation from CO2 and nitrate on Cu. Among Li+, Na+, K+, and Cs+, K+ affords the lowest calculated barrier for direct *CO–*NO coupling and the highest measured urea Faradaic efficiency. Varying the K+ concentration reveals a volcano‐shaped dependence of urea activity and selectivity, with a maximum at a partial current density of 13.62 mA cm−2 and Faradaic efficiency of 24.50% near 1.20 M K+. AIMD calculations identify a minimum coupling barrier at an intermediate nominal K+ concentration and elucidate how K+ concentration regulates precursor geometry and charge redistribution. Complementary cMD simulations reveal concentration‐dependent changes in interfacial reactant distributions and water structure, with infrared spectral features providing experimental evidence of changes in interfacial reaction chemistry. Together, these results establish an optimal K+ concentration window governed by the coupled roles of elementary‐step kinetics and electrolyte organization in urea electrosynthesis.

title: Dynamic Soft‐Confinement via Hydrogen‐Bonded Organic Frameworks Reshapes C–C Coupling Interfacial Chemistry at Bi1–Bi2 Sites
content:
A dynamic soft‐confinement catalytic strategy by in situ constructing a disordered HOF layer on Bi3O4Br surfaces has been proposed to boost C–C coupling from CO2 photoreduction.








ABSTRACT
The core bottleneck in photocatalytic CO2 reduction toward multi‐carbon oxygenates lies in the thermodynamic‐kinetic dual limitations of the C–C coupling step. Conventional strategies have focused on intrinsic electronic structure optimization of active sites while overlooking the critical influence of the reaction microenvironment on coupling probability. Herein, we propose a dynamic soft‐confinement catalytic strategy by in situ constructing a disordered hydrogen‐bonded organic framework (HOF) layer on Bi3O4Br surfaces, thereby establishing an HOF/Bi3O4Br integrated photocatalytic system. The introduction of HOF not only induces the formation of asymmetric Bi1–Bi2 coupling sites but also establishes a dynamic hydrogen‐bonding microenvironment surrounding them. This microenvironment enhances CO2 coverage near the coupling sites by constructing a persistent carbon source enrichment layer. Simultaneously, the interfacial polarization field promotes exciton dissociation and directs electron transport toward the Bi1–Bi2 sites. Furthermore, the reconfigurable hydrogen bonds impose orientational soft confinement on *CO intermediates, guiding them into spatial configurations favorable for *OCCO bond formation. This soft‐hard synergistic interfacial design enables 0.7HOF/Bi3O4Br to achieve a CH3COOH production rate of 325.12 µmol g−1 h−1 with 98.81% product selectivity under sacrificial agent‐free conditions. This work demonstrates that dynamic microenvironment programming around active sites constitutes a critical pathway for overcoming the photocatalytic C–C coupling bottleneck.

title: Lewis Acid–Base Pairs in Photo/Electrocatalysis: Cooperative Mechanisms, Design Strategies, and Applications
content:
Lewis acid–base pairs (LPs) provide synergistic dual active sites for regulating electron transfer and molecular activation. This review summarizes the mechanisms, construction, characterization and applications of LPs in photo/electrocatalytic energy conversion and environmental remediation, together with future opportunities for rational LPs design.








ABSTRACT
Developing high‐performance and robust catalysts is essential for advancing photo/electrocatalytic technologies for sustainable energy conversion and environmental remediation. Single‐component catalysts inherently suffer from linear scaling relations in electrocatalysis and the trade‐off between light‐response scope and redox abilities in photocatalysis, failing to dynamically modulate adsorption strength of multiple intermediates. To circumvent these thermodynamic limitations, the precise introduction of Lewis acid–base pairs (LPs), specifically frustrated Lewis pairs (FLPs), has emerged as a sophisticated strategy to overcome the inherent trade‐off between activity and stability. By modulating the spatial and electronic synergy between electron‐accepting (Lewis acid) and electron‐donating (Lewis base) sites, LPs enable unique small‐molecule activation mechanisms. This dual‐site cooperative synergy provides tailored adsorption strengths for diverse reaction intermediates and significantly reduces kinetic energy barriers, thereby enhancing both catalytic activity and stability. This review critically elucidates the fundamental mechanisms and design principles of LPs in photo/electrocatalysis, and systematically highlights their crucial applications in sustainable energy conversion and environmental remediation. Finally, we outline the remaining challenges, emphasizing the necessity of coupling advanced characterization with density functional theory calculations to unravel dynamic structure‐activity relationships, thereby guiding the rational design of LPs‐engineered catalytic systems for practical applications.

title: From Synapses to Security: Morphological Transformation Organic Electrochemical Transistors for Edge Intelligence
content:
A morphology‐driven dual‐mode organic electrochemical transistor is presented, which provides one‐way functional conversion from synaptic computing to hardware security through a simple solvent treatment. The morphological transformation leads to distinct synaptic and physical unclonable function.








ABSTRACT
Neuromorphic computing and hardware‐level security are both critical for next‐generation edge intelligence systems, yet integrating these functions within a single device remains challenging because synaptic operation requires uniform conductance modulation, whereas physical unclonable functions (PUFs) rely on intrinsic randomness. Here, we report a morphology‐driven dual‐mode organic electrochemical transistor (OECT) based on a P3HT:PBA:Triton X‐100 blended active layer that undergoes a one‐way functional conversion from synaptic to PUF operation through a simple acetone soaking process. In the synaptic mode, the device exhibits a ∼20‐fold higher long‐term memory (LTM) value than the P3HT‐based OECT and a paired‐pulse facilitation index of up to 180%. In addition, Pavlovian associative learning and reservoir computing were demonstrated using the experimentally measured synaptic responses. Following solvent‐induced morphological transformation, the device exhibits device‐to‐device electrical variations, exhibiting PUF metrics of ∼50% uniformity, an average inter‐HD of 50.89%, and an entropy of 0.99. These results demonstrate that morphology‐driven functional conversion enables synaptic and PUF functions to be realized within a common organic electronic platform.

title: Single‐Vesicle Functional Nanophenotyping Reveals Heterogeneous PD‐L1 Accessibility in Triple‐Negative Breast Cancer (Small Methods 22/2026)
content:

High‐speed atomic force microscopy reveals how anti‐PD‐L1 antibodies dynamically engage individual tumour‐derived extracellular vesicles. Single‐vesicle functional nanophenotyping uncovers striking heterogeneity in PD‐L1 accessibility, distinguishing persistent from transient antibody interactions. The cover illustrates this nanoscale landscape, where extracellular vesicles released from cancer cells encounter antibodies under the probing tip of high‐speed AFM, revealing their functional surface diversity. title: Downsize Effect on Photocatalytic Syngas Production of a 2D Metal Organic Framework—Tuning the Selectivity From HER to CO2RR via Dimensional Modulation and Mechanical Exfoliation of 2D Metal‐Organic Layers (Small Methods 22/2026)
content:
Back Cover
Tuning the selectivity from hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) to CO2 reduction is highly desirable. In article number e70843, Rajat Saha, Debmalya Ray, Hermenegildo García Gómez, Carlos J. Gómez García, and co‐workers have prepared a 2D metal–organic framework (MOF) and converted it into a 1D MOF via dehydration‐rehydration and into an exfoliated 2D MOF by liquid phase exfoliation. Photocatalytic CO2 reduction shows that the bulk 2D MOF has higher selectivity for HER while the 1D and exfoliated MOFs show CO enriched syngas production.

title: Superoxide Dismutase‐Functionalized Titanium Dioxide Colloidosomes for Enhanced UV Protection and Persistent ROS Suppression
content:
SOD‐functionalized TiO2 colloidosomes (STCs) are self‐assembled from SOD‐adsorbed TiO2 nanoparticles for enhanced UV protection and persistent ROS suppression. The hollow mesoporous shell enhances UV shielding, while interfacially immobilized SOD scavenges photogenerated superoxide in situ. STCs maintain >95% ROS inhibition over repeated UV irradiation and show low cytotoxicity in the tested HaCaT cells, offering a durable antioxidant strategy for TiO2‐based UV filters. 








ABSTRACT
Titanium dioxide (TiO2), serving as a prominent inorganic ultraviolet (UV) filter, has been widely utilized in photoprotective formulations. However, its photocatalytic activity under UV irradiation generates reactive oxygen species (ROS), thereby raising significant concerns regarding photochemical safety. Although antioxidant coatings have been proposed to suppress TiO2‐induced ROS, persistent ROS suppression remains challenging due to the intrinsically sacrificial nature of conventional antioxidant components. Herein, we report an efficient strategy for constructing superoxide dismutase (SOD)‐functionalized TiO2 colloidosomes (STCs) for persistent ROS suppression. SOD is first electrostatically adsorbed onto TiO2 nanoparticles, followed by droplet‐confined self‐assembly of the resulting SOD–TiO2 nanoparticles into hollow mesoporous colloidosomes. This hierarchical design enables in situ scavenging of photogenerated ROS at the TiO2 interface while stabilizing SOD. Compared with bare TiO2 NPs, the STCs exhibit an approximately 1.81‐fold enhancement in Sun Protection Factor (SPF). Moreover, the STCs maintain ROS inhibition efficiencies above 95% over three consecutive 6 h UV irradiation cycles and exhibit low cytotoxicity in the tested HaCaT cells. This study provides a feasible strategy for the development of TiO2‐based UV filtration materials that integrate enhanced UV protection with persistent enzymatic antioxidant functionality, highlighting their potential applications in advanced photoprotective materials and sunscreen formulations for human health.

title: Tunable diffusive memristor arrays for neuromorphic temporal computing
content:
Nature Materials, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41563-026-02815-z

Scaling diffusive memristors from single devices to integrated systems has been hindered by stochastic ionic motion and filament evolution. Here confined metal-ion migration enables controlled relaxation dynamics, as demonstrated in a 28 × 14 array for neuromorphic computing.
journal: Nature Materials

title: The power of O vacancies in electrocatalysis
content:
Nature Chemistry, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41557-026-02316-1

Non-stoichiometric oxide materials are essential to chemistry, but controlling their synthesis towards a tuneable number of unpaired electrons trapped in the oxygen vacancies remains challenging. Now, a new synthetic strategy leveraging template chemicals renders these materials available for electron-driven electrocatalytic selectivity.
journal: Nature Chemistry

title: Binuclear copper enzymes enable selective radical (pseudo)halogenation
content:
Nature Chemistry, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41557-026-02311-6

Synthetically valuable new-to-nature reactions in copper enzymes remain largely underexploited in chemical synthesis. Now, the combination of binuclear copper enzymes and a photoredox catalyst can efficiently perform enantioselective decarboxylative (pseudo)halogenation starting from redox-active esters.
journal: Nature Chemistry

title: Comprehensive synthesis of K48/K63 ubiquitin pentamers by graph-empowered automation
content:
Nature Chemistry, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41557-026-02312-5

The combinatorial space of ubiquitin chains hampers their preparation and study. Now, synthetic and computational tools have been developed for comprehensive access to all 56 K48/K63-linked ubiquitin tetramers and pentamers. This work uses advances in the chemical synthesis of selectively protected ubiquitin monomers, graph-based encoding of ubiquitin chains, and automated procedures.
journal: Nature Chemistry

title: Learning beyond rigid manipulation with hybrid soft-rigid robots
content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79571-w

Rigid robots are precise but struggle to adapt, while soft robots are flexible but less reliable. Here, the authors show that a hybrid soft-rigid robot can learn varied manipulation tasks from one demonstration, combining precision with adaptability.

content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79752-7

content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79543-0

The study shows that disagreements among global urban growth projections can substantially affect future deforestation and carbon emissions estimates, revealing a key source of uncertainty in land and climate assessments.

title: Nuclear factor I connects H3K27M to a targetable purine dependency in diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma
content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79694-0

Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma is an aggressive childhood cancer commonly driven by H3K27M with few treatment options. This study links H3K27M-driven chromatin remodelling to NFI-dependent purine metabolism, causing ATIC/PNP-mediated metabolic rewiring and ATIC-targetable tumour dependence.

title: Plant protoplasts display phytopodia
content:
Nature Communications, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79550-1

Plant cells are encased in cell walls that when digested leave spherical protoplasts. Here the authors report long, thin membrane protrusions from protoplasts termed phytopodia and discuss their potential role in the probing behaviour of the cell cortex.

title: Chemical defects in semiconducting polymers and their impact on reproducibility and device performance
content:
Nature Reviews Materials, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41578-026-00984-6

Synthesizing semiconducting polymers often introduces structural defects, altering optoelectronic properties and directly impairing device performance. This Perspective details defect origins, evaluation methods and mitigation strategies, demonstrating how controlling structural variability resolves batch-to-batch inconsistency while unlocking novel materials design opportunities.
journal: Nature Reviews Materials

title: Coupled hydrogen spillover and CO2 activation sites in high-entropy catalysts for CO2 reduction
content: Converting CO2 into useful chemicals via reverse water-gas shift reaction offers a promising route toward sustainable carbon utilization. However, catalysts often struggle to coordinate hydrogen and CO2 activation while remaining stable under demanding reaction conditions. The present work developed high-entropy oxides with Li and Al dual-atom doping to promote cooperative alloy-oxide interfaces with coupled H2 and CO2 activation sites, thereby enabling fast, selective, and stable CO production. These findings provide a general strategy for integrating multiple functions into robust catalysts for challenging chemical transformations.
journal: Chem

title:
Electrochemical Allylic
Carboxylation of Unactivated
Alkenes with CO2
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As both alkenes and CO2 are abundant and easily available feedstocks, carboxylation of alkenes with CO2 represents an attractive and sustainable strategy to synthesize value-added carboxylic acids. Despite substantial advances in carboxylation of π-bonds in alkenes, the carboxylation of C–H bonds in alkenes, which preserves the C═C bond in the synthesis of valuable unsaturated carboxylic acids, remains a longstanding challenge, particularly for unactivated alkenes owing to their intrinsically low reactivity. Herein, we report the first electrochemical allylic carboxylation of unactivated alkenes with CO2, providing a direct and selective approach to hard-to-obtain β,γ-unsaturated carboxylic acids. Moreover, this reaction exhibits a broad substrate scope, good functional group tolerance, and applicability to late-stage diversification. Mechanistic studies indicate that the electrogenerated CO2 radical anion acts both as the carboxylation reagent and the hydrogen-atom abstraction species for the subsequent desaturation process, further uncovering the synthetic utility potential of the CO2 radical anion.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
A Bioinspired
Thiolate-Bridged Diiron System for Functionally
Replicating Hydrazine Dehydrogenase and Its Efficient Electrocatalytic
Hydrazine Oxidation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hydrazine dehydrogenase (HDH) catalyzes the oxidation of hydrazine (N2H4) to dinitrogen (N2) as the final step of anaerobic ammonium oxidation, an essential process in closing the nitrogen cycle. Despite extensive biochemical studies, the detailed mechanism of HDH at a molecular level remains elusive. An increasing number of studies indicate that the hydrazine oxidation reaction (HzOR) is also central to direct hydrazine fuel cells. However, known electrocatalysts for HzOR are predominantly heterogeneous systems, while molecular electrocatalysts are still scarce, especially those inspired by biological HDH. This scarcity not only limits mechanistic understanding but also hinders the development of efficient and tunable catalysts. To tackle these challenging issues, we sought inspiration from the biological HDH system, wherein multiple iron-containing heme subunits cooperatively promote efficient HzOR with the assistance of surrounding sulfur-bearing cysteine residues. Integrating these key features, we selected the thiolate-bridged diiron complex [Cp*Fe(μ-SEt)(MeCN)]2[PF6]2 (1, Cp* = η5-C5Me5) for functionally replicating HDH. Treatment of 1 with N2H4 induces disproportionation to afford the active diazene (N2H2) species, which can be captured by the diiron cooperative platform to yield [Cp*Fe(μ-SEt)2(cis-μ-η1:η1-HN=NH)FeCp*][PF6] (2). In the presence of appropriate electron and proton acceptors, complex 2 undergoes a two-electron oxidation, leading to N2 release and the regeneration of 1. Remarkably, both complexes 1 and 2 serve as efficient molecular electrocatalysts for HzOR. This diiron molecular system not only achieves the functional replication of HDH involving a key N2H2 intermediate but also establishes a bioinspired design strategy for developing multimetal cooperative electrocatalysts toward efficient HzOR.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Strengthening Metal–Oxygen
Bonds via Ionicity–Covalency
Asymmetric Connection: 4f Electronic Configuration Effect
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Precise control over the characteristics of metal–oxygen (M–O) bonds by regulating the electron redistribution between the metal and oxygen under perturbation conditions is crucial for maintaining the structural stability of transition-metal oxides. However, its development has always been hindered by the strong coupling between orbital hybridization and charge localization. Herein, by leveraging the strong ionicity of the Ce–O bonds in CeO2, we constructed an ionicity–covalency asymmetric bonding network, in which the ionic Ce–O is atomically coupled with the covalent M–O (M = Ni/Co). The reduced Ce–O coordination in this special structure weakens the O 2p → Ce 4f charge transfer and further elevates the ionic character of Ce–O bonds, thereby activating the reversible 4f electronic configuration transition. Critically, this configuration undergoes reversible transformation under potential fluctuation, reshaping charge redistribution within the M–O bonding motifs and then suppressing irreversible M–O bond degradation. Harnessing this mechanism enables transition-metal oxides to express a robust framework for the whole structure under repeated redox cycling. Incorporating this resulting CeO2/NiCo2O4, a large-scale alkaline water electrolysis (AWE) stack delivers significantly stable operation for over 350 h at 6 A under a 12-h intermittent experimental protocol. This finding offers a fundamental insight into the dynamic charge distribution in M–O bonds under potential perturbation for universal structural protection.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title: Revisiting the Biosynthetic Cyclization of Indole Sesquiterpene Alkaloids: Proposal of a Spiro -Indolenine Pathway and Synthesis of Prelecanindole
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Indole sesquiterpene and indole diterpene alkaloids constitute a distinctive class of natural products characterized by complex polycyclic ring architectures and diverse potent biological activities. In indole sesquiterpenes, the characteristic indole-containing pentacyclic skeleton is biosynthesized from 3-farnesylindole through epoxidation followed by a sequential cationic cyclization. Although the cyclization enzyme has been identified, the details of its cyclization mechanism remain unclear. Here, we propose a new biosynthetic mechanism involving a spiro-indoleninium intermediate, which contrasts with the long-standing mechanism proposed in the 1970s that proceeds via a tertiary-to-secondary carbocation rearrangement. We demonstrated the feasibility of this new mechanism by means of density functional theory (DFT) calculations, which do not support the conventional mechanism and also by chemical emulation: the putative spiro-indolenine intermediate was synthesized from two fragments through stereoselective cyclopropanation as a key reaction and subsequently converted to prelecanindole, a common biosynthetic intermediate of indole sesquiterpene alkaloids, under mild acidic conditions.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Electron-Deficient
β-Diketone Ligand
Enabled Ni-Catalyzed Remote Dicarbofunctionalization of Alkenes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A nickel-catalyzed remote migratory dicarbofunctionalization of alkenes was realized with high efficiency and excellent regioselectivity without the assistance of a directing group. The formation of a thermodynamically stable allyl-metal intermediate and the use of an electron-deficient β-diketone ligand are the keys to the success of these remote diarylation and arylalkenylation. This protocol features a broad substrate scope and excellent functional group compatibility, providing a series of remote diarylated and arylalkenylated hydrocarbons in high yields. Notably, the allyl group represents one of the most synthetically useful handles in synthetic chemistry, and the synthetic values of this process have been demonstrated by the formal synthesis of allocolchicinoids, and by the preparation of a RARγ selective retinoid agonist in a highly efficient and step-economical manner.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Single-Atom Cerium
Unlocks Efficient Hydrogen Spillover
within Nonreducible Zeolites through a Proton–Electron Relay
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hydrogen spillover connects hydrogen activation with spatially separated catalytic functions, yet engineering efficient hydrogen transport through nonreducible zeolites remains an outstanding challenge owing to the absence of intrinsic pathways for coupled proton–electron transfer. Here, we show that isolated cerium atoms incorporated into Pt/USY transform the zeolite from a passive support into an active medium for solid-state hydrogen transport. In situ spectroscopy, isotopic tracing, and theoretical calculations reveal that atomically dispersed Ce species dynamically generate localized hydroxyl groups and oxygen vacancies that cooperatively establish a proton–electron relay, substantially lowering the kinetic barrier for hydrogen migration through zeolitic micropores. The resulting enhancement in hydrogen spillover extends hydrogen delivery to spatially remote Brønsted acid sites, suppresses coke formation, and significantly improves polyolefin hydrocracking stability. These findings establish hydrogen transport as a tunable design parameter in bifunctional zeolite catalysis and provide a general strategy for engineering hydrogen-transfer pathways in nonreducible porous materials.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Synthetic Control of
Quantum Phases in Organic Conductors:
Molecular-Level Disorder Engineering and Pressure-Induced Superconductivity
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Structural randomness is a dominant factor governing electronic properties; however, the intrinsic effects of a disordered potential remain elusive due to the lack of a synthetic platform capable of introducing purely random potentials without carrier doping or altering the fundamental band structure. Here, we demonstrate the synthetic control of superconducting and insulating phases by exploiting the unique conformational flexibility of molecular conductors. Through precise thermodynamic control during crystal growth, we selectively synthesize the structurally ordered superconductor κ-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu[N(CN)2]Br (κ-Br; BEDT-TTF = bis(ethylenedithio)tetrathiafulvalene) and the structurally disordered insulating polymorph, κ″-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu[N(CN)2]Br (κ″-Br), possessing the exact same chemical composition. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations confirm the metastable nature of κ″-Br, showing a packing arrangement of BEDT-TTF molecules and an electronic band structure nearly identical to those of superconducting κ-Br, but featuring a disordered anion layer. Optical conductivity spectra reveal low-energy excitations without a distinct gap, indicating that the insulating behavior originates from disorder-induced carrier localization. Furthermore, κ″-Br undergoes a pressure-induced insulator–superconductor transition, in stark contrast to postsynthetic X-ray irradiation which induced irreversible structural damage. This work represents the first demonstration of synthetic control of an ordered superconductor and a disordered insulator driven solely by orientational disorder in organic conductors. Our study provides new avenues for manipulating strongly correlated electron systems and for investigating the intrinsic effects of randomness, free from carrier doping or structural perturbation of conducting layers.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Redox-Window-Guided
Metal Node Editing of Copper Metal–Organic
Frameworks for Recyclable Heterogeneous Cu(I) Catalysis
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cu(I) catalysts are central to many bond-forming reactions, but integrating Cu(I) sites into recyclable porous solids remains difficult because Cu(I) is easily oxidized, over-reduced, or leached. Here, we report redox-window-guided metal node editing as an oxidation-state-programming strategy that converts hydrolytically fragile Cu(II)3BTC2 into a hydrolytically stable mixed-valence Cu(I/II) MOF catalyst. Phenolic reductants are selected by matching their oxidation potentials to the Cu(II)–to–Cu(I) window of Cu(II)3BTC2, enabling proton-coupled, inner-sphere single-electron transfer at Cu paddlewheel nodes. Hydroquinone gives the most controlled material, [p-Ph(OH)2]-Cu3BTC2, containing 33.4% Cu(I), ship-in-a-bottle [Cu(MeCN)4]+ complexes, mesopores, and enhanced stability under humid, acidic, and basic conditions. As a heterogeneous catalyst for hydrative amide synthesis, [p-Ph(OH)2]-Cu3BTC2 affords 92% yield, negligible Cu leaching, five-cycle recyclability, and the highest turnover number among compared Cu(I) catalysts.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Hydrogen-Bond Network-Assisted
Ethylene and Hydrogen
Photosynthesis from Methane over Isolated Ir Active Sites under Ambient
Conditions
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Direct conversion of methane to ethylene (DCM) is an attractive yet formidable challenge due to the difficult C–H activation and uncontrollable C–C coupling process. Herein, we report a hydrogen-bond network-assisted ethylene and H2 photosynthesis from methane over oxygen-vacancy-enriched TiO2-supported single Ir atoms (Ir1/TiO2–Ov) under ambient conditions. The Ir-induced lattice distortion drives spontaneous hydrolysis under humid conditions, generating a hydroxylated surface that endows coordinatively unsaturated Ir sites to activate the first methane molecule without light irradiation. Upon photoexcitation, surface hydroxyls are oxidized into dangling oxygen species (*O) on Ti sites, which promote the dehydrogenation of *CH3 to *CH2. In synergy with the Ir site, the adjacent *O species activate a second CH4 molecule and finally direct selective C–C coupling to form C2H4. Meanwhile, methane-derived protons migrate through the hydrogen-bond network via a Grotthuss mechanism to produce H2. The Ir1/TiO2–Ov catalyst achieves the production of ethylene (14.3 ± 0.7 μmol•gcat–1•h–1) and H2 (28.4 ± 1.2 μmol•gcat–1•h–1) for at least 210 h at 25 °C and atmospheric pressure under light irradiation. Our findings establish a hydrogen-bond network-assisted strategy for methane C–H activation and selective C–C and H–H coupling.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Stepwise
Assembly of a Lavandulyl Moiety on Flavonoids
Enabled by a 2″-Prenyltransferase
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Lavandulylated flavonoids contain a characteristic branched C10 moiety, and the enzymatic basis underlying its biosynthesis remains poorly understood. Here, we elucidate the complete biosynthetic pathway of the lavandulylated flavonoid kurarinone from naringenin in the medicinal plant Sophora flavescens. The pathway involves four sequential steps, 8-prenylation, 2′-hydroxylation, 2″-prenylation, and 5-O-methylation, catalyzed by Sf8PT, SfF2′H, Sf2″PT, and Sf5OMT, respectively. Sf2′′PT represents the first characterized flavonoid 2′′-prenyltransferase (PT), catalyzing a second prenylation on the pre-existing prenyl side chain to complete the assembly of the branched lavandulyl moiety. The activity of Sf2″PT strictly depends on prior 2′-hydroxylation, establishing a defined order of enzymatic modifications that enables this noncanonical prenylation reaction. Ancestral sequence reconstruction and mutagenesis demonstrated that an inactive ancestral enzyme could be converted into functional 8PT or 2′′PT variants through one or seven amino acid substitutions, respectively. Collectively, this work establishes the enzymatic basis for stepwise lavandulyl moiety assembly and provides a framework for the enzymatic construction and engineering of branched prenylated natural products.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Departing Pathways
in Aza-Diarylethene Photoswitching:
Elucidating the Role of the Central Ring Allows Reprogramming of the
Photoresponse
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Aza-diarylethenes (aza-DAEs) are an emerging class of molecular photoswitches that allow reversible C–N bond formation and cleavage upon irradiation. They not only show high potential as T-type photochromes but also offer exciting opportunities for the exploration of unique reactivity control. Two types of these photoswitches are currently being investigated, which differ substantially in the nature of their metastable states. While classical DAE behavior is found in perfluorinated thiazole derivatives, an unexpected zwitterion formation and concomitant aromatization is observed for nonfluorinated pyrimidine derivatives. The latter offers reversible control over intramolecular charge separation and intrinsic three-state photoswitching. Their metastable state unleashes thiolate reactivity, which can be harnessed, e.g., in photoinitiation applications for smart polymer generation. Despite this promising progress, the reason for the divergent photochemical behavior in aza-DAEs is not yet understood. Here, we show that substitution of the central five-membered ring is responsible for the different photochemical outcomes and nature of the metastable state. Furthermore, our computational results provide systematic insights into the structural factors governing the relative stability of the neutral closed-ring and zwitterionic forms. We then use this knowledge to reprogram thioazole derivatives and render them into zwitterion-forming aza-DAEs. With these results, the predictable and rational design of aza-DAEs is enabled, which can now be radically changed in their photoresponses and tailored to specific desired properties and applications.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Rh2C3− Cluster-Driven
Nitrogen Activation: Trapping a High-Energy Intermediate
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Converting inert and globally abundant molecules such as N2 into useful chemicals is central to sustainable energy and environmental chemistry. Herein, we investigate the gas-phase reaction of the Rh2C3− anion with N2 using mass spectrometry, anion photoelectron spectroscopy, and quantum chemical calculations. The experimental spectra of Rh2C3− and Rh2C3N2− exhibit closely similar features, indicating a preserved electronic core upon N2 attachment. Theoretical analysis further reveals that the end-on N2 adsorption complex is a trapped high-energy intermediate whose subsequent transformation is prevented by an activation barrier that necessitates additional energy input, and that this complex exhibits superior performance in the coconversion of diverse energy-bearing gas molecules. Furthermore, the subsequent application of oriented external electric fields provides a nondestructive and continuously adjustable means of modifying the intrinsic barrier heights, thereby effectively switching the reaction mechanism. These findings elucidate the complex reaction network of Rh2C3− with N2, establish a reliable spectroscopic fingerprint for identifying isomeric intermediates, and provide fundamental insights into electronic control strategies for catalytic nitrogen activation.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Antibody-Guided
Photocatalytic Cross-Linking Enables
Targeted Protein Structure Elucidation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The structure and dynamics of proteins underlie virtually all biological processes, and there is a growing need for methods that can interrogate protein conformations in complex mixtures. Chemical cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) addresses this need. Still, it relies on untargeted, diffusible cross-linkers that react with any accessible residue, limiting both selectivity and effective use of cross-linking capacity. Here, we report an antibody-guided, photocatalytic cross-linking platform that enables targeted structural elucidation of proteins of interest within complex samples. We developed HyProX, a trifunctional histidine-specific cross-linker that combines two hydrazide groups to trap light-induced histidine intermediates and a phosphonic acid handle for enrichment. Building on LUX-MS photocatalytic proximity labeling, singlet oxygen generators (SOGs) conjugated to antibodies locally convert histidines on the target protein into short-lived endoperoxide intermediates, which HyProX selectively captures to form His–His cross-links in a strictly light-dependent manner. Using model peptides, we demonstrate efficient formation of cross-linked products and show that HyProX forms a C–N bond that undergoes preferential collision-induced dissociation (CID), releasing signature fragment pairs that MS3 can directly sequence. Applying antibody-guided HyProX cross-linking to human transferrin in a multiprotein mixture and human serum yields an increase in cross-linked spectral matches and higher unique cross-link coverage for the target protein compared to untargeted conditions, with all observed cross-links mapping on the known crystal structure. Together, these results establish antibody-guided, photocatalytic His–His cross-linking with HyProX as a conceptually new XL-MS platform that provides spatiotemporal control, residue selectivity, and an intrinsic MS-based decross-linking readout for targeted protein structure analysis in complex biological mixtures.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Nucleotide-Resolved
Conformational Analysis of Nascent
RNA Chains within the Bacterial Transcription Elongation Complex by
MAS-DNP Solid-State NMR
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In all kingdoms of life, multisubunit RNA polymerases transcribe DNA to RNA. Both genomic DNA and newly transcribed RNA play key roles in transcription initiation, elongation, and termination. For example, a stretch of uridine residues at the 3′-end of the nascent RNA chain serves as a trigger to terminate transcription, release the nascent RNA chain, and disassemble bacterial transcription elongation complexes (ECs). It has remained unclear how the transcript can trigger termination if polyuridine stretches are synthesized. Here, we establish an approach that combines site-selective 13C/15N labeling of uridines with magic-angle-spinning dynamic nuclear polarization (MAS-DNP) NMR to probe the nascent transcript residue by residue within a reconstituted, stalled Escherichia coli transcription EC. We read out the 3′-terminal U-tract in the free RNA and in complexes stalled at two registers to investigate conformational heterogeneity in the rU–dA hybrid duplex. Our results suggest that the internal uridines adopt a stable A-form (C3′-endo) conformation in the hybrid duplex. This conformation remains unchanged within the EC, whereas the 3′-terminal residue is selectively perturbed within the complex. Solid-state NMR data collected on tailored isotopically labeled ECs resolve single-residue differences in conformation inside an assembled transcription EC, opening a route to study the nascent RNA at sites relevant to pausing and termination by MAS-DNP.</jats:p>

title: Spatial Confinement Enables In Situ Growth of the Nano-Sn@Sn3(PO4)2 Anode for Sodium-Ion Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nanoarchitecturing improves capacity utilization and mitigates mechanical stress of Sn anodes for elevated energy density sodium-ion batteries (SIBs), yet substantial surface energy induces nanoparticle aggregation. Traditional heterotopic coatings cannot sustain long-term mechanical confinement upon repeated volume variation of Sn. Herein, we propose a dealloying-induced phase transformation and spatial confinement strategy to in situ construct a robust Sn3(PO4)2 coating on Sn nanoparticles. Sn3(PO4)2 provides spatial confinement for the homogeneously dispersed Sn nanoparticles, while the nano-Sn (∼20 nm) within the Sn3(PO4)2 framework effectively alleviates mechanical stress and suppresses volume expansion. Consequently, Sn@Sn3(PO4)2 exhibits attractive structural integrity and electrochemical performance, with a reversible capacity of 772 mAh g–1, 83% capacity retention after 3600 cycles, and 583 mAh g–1 at 5 A g–1. Moreover, the Sn@Sn3(PO4)2||Na3V2(PO4)3 full cell delivers a favorable cycling stability and rate performance. This in situ reconstruction strategy guides electrode surface engineering and facilitates the application of Sn-based anodes in future SIBs.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Programming Sodium-Storage Kinetics through Linear Quinone Oligomerization
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quinone-based organic cathodes enable reversible multielectron redox reactions but suffer from dissolution and sluggish sodium-storage kinetics. Here, two structurally homologous linear quinone oligomers, biphenyl–quinone dimer (2BQ) and terphenyl–quinone trimer (3BQ), are compared to elucidate how backbone extension regulates sodium storage. Compared with 2BQ, 3BQ exhibits reduced crystallinity, enhanced electrochemical utilization, a narrower HOMO–LUMO gap, and lower oxidation reorganization energy. Consequently, 3BQ delivers a reversible capacity of 350 mA h g–1 at 0.05C and retains 80% of its capacity after 500 cycles at 1C, with enhanced rate capability and cycling stability. Operando FTIR and state-dependent XPS reveal reversible C=O/C–O–Na conversion, while density functional theory calculations elucidate an extended multielectron sodiation sequence. These findings establish controlled linear quinone oligomerization as an effective, rational molecular design strategy to reduce apparent dissolution tendency and improve carbonyl-site utilization and sodium-storage kinetics, providing insights into the development of advanced organic cathodes for rechargeable sodium-ion batteries.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Energy Letters

title: Liquid Metal Interlayers Enable Zero-Pressure Sulfide Solid Electrolyte Lithium Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Lithium metal anodes are essential for high-energy-density batteries with solid-state electrolytes (SSEs), but the lithium-SSE interface suffers from contact loss and current constriction during cycling. External stack pressure can enhance contact retention but adds system-level limitations and accelerates lithium filament penetration. Here, a room-temperature liquid sodium–potassium (NaK) interlayer is demonstrated to stabilize the lithium–sulfide SSE interface under nominally zero stack pressure by combining stress-free morphological adaptability with Li transport capability. In situ X-ray computed tomography and other analytical methods reveal that the liquid layer reconfigures to preserve interfacial contact during Li plating/stripping. Finite Li solubility in the NaK also creates a dissolved-Li-mediated electrochemical pathway that supports Li stripping from a distant reservoir. The dual mechanical and transport functions of NaK enable stable full-cell cycling (600 cycles, &gt;2 mAh cm–2) with layered-oxide composite cathodes under nominally zero applied stack pressure. These findings highlight a fundamental interfacial design concept based on a compliant interlayer that accommodates morphological evolution while supporting Li transport under minimal mechanical confinement.</jats:p>

title: Polymerizable ionic buffers transform grain boundaries into ion-regulating interfaces in metal halide perovskites
content: Long-term operational instability remains a critical barrier for perovskite photovoltaics toward commercial deployment, originating largely from uncontrolled ionic migration across grain boundaries. Mobile A-site cations and halide ions transform grain boundaries in metal-halide perovskites into nanoscale ion-transport pathways, undermining device stability. Here, we develop a polymerizable imidazolium tetrafluoroborate ionic buffer that chemically stabilizes mobile A- and X-site species while physically confining grain-boundary pathways. The BF4− counterion interacts with undercoordinated Pb sites, whereas the propargyl-substituted imidazolium cation stabilizes organic A-site cations, suppresses deprotonation, and scavenges reactive iodine species. Upon post-deposition activation, the cation undergoes in situ polymerization within grain-boundary regions to form an amorphous intergranular network. Correlative nanoscale characterization reveals reduced ion redistribution, electrostatic heterogeneity, and local electrical hysteresis. The inverted perovskite solar cells reach 27.25% efficiency (certified 27.03%), while 13.95 cm2 modules achieve a certified 24.10% efficiency and retain 95% of their initial performance after 2000 h of continuous maximum power point tracking. Outdoor testing supports the practical viability of this grain-boundary protection strategy.

title: Anode-free configurations through separator-mediated interfacial regulation for practical sodium metal batteries
content: Separator-mediated interfacial regulation has emerged as a central design principle for enabling high-performance sodium metal batteries, particularly in anode-free configurations where reversibility must be achieved without excess sodium. This Review outlines how functionally engineered separators, rather than acting as passive barriers, can regulate Na+ transport, homogenize ion flux, stabilize the solid–electrolyte interphase, and suppress dendritic growth under increasingly stringent operating conditions. We discuss the interfacial origins of failure in conventional and anode-free sodium metal batteries, define the key physicochemical requirements of separators, and survey passive and functional architectures across structural, chemical, and bio-derived design spaces. We pay special attention to separator strategies that couple mechanical adaptation with solvation control and field-assisted ion regulation, reconciling rapid transport with interfacial stability. Finally, we highlight emerging separator concepts for anode-free systems and identify the major challenges that remain for practical deployment, including scalability, durability, and validation under realistic cell conditions. Together, these advances establish separators as active interfacial regulators and point to a broadly applicable pathway toward safer, higher-energy sodium metal batteries.

title: Reversible liquid-phase lithium transfer across the battery lifecycle
content: Lithium underpins high-energy-density batteries and has become strategically critical for sustainable energy transitions. Conventional solid lithium sources used in battery manufacturing suffer from poor interfacial contact, heterogeneous lithium delivery and limited diffusion kinetics, constraining production efficiency and material utilisation. Lithium–arene complexes (LACs), formed by the reversible reaction between lithium and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), provide a liquid-phase route for lithium transfer. In this review, we describe the PAH/LAC pair as two chemical states of a reversible lithium carrier, where PAH represents the Li-depleted state and LAC the Li-loaded state. We first discuss the fundamental chemistry of PAH/LAC conversion and the factors determining LAC reduction potential, including PAH structure, solvent environment, temperature and concentration. We then summarise the applications of PAH-based lithium extraction, including lithium-based foil fabrication, lithium-alloy modification and quantitative analysis of inactive lithium, followed by LAC-based lithium donation for anode and cathode pre-lithiation, electrode and cell-level lithium supplementation, spent-cathode regeneration and the synthesis of lithium-containing materials. These processes are further evaluated in terms of reaction time, process efficiency, lithium utilisation, material compatibility and process requirements. Particular attention is given to the recovery and reuse of PAHs and solvents, and to the possibility of transferring lithium recovered from one process directly to another. Finally, we discuss molecular design, process integration and closed-loop lithium transfer as directions towards practical implementation of the PAH/LAC pair across the battery lifecycle.

In article number e71467, Chengcheng Fang and co‐workers reveal that moisture stability in Na3PS4 is governed by competition between dehydration and hydrolysis. Under limited moisture exposure, thermal treatment removes absorbed water and largely restores ionic conductivity, whereas severe exposure promotes irreversible hydrolysis. These findings establish a kinetic basis for moisture tolerance and recovery in sulfide solid electrolytes.

title: Antigen‐Presenting Microrobots Program CAR‐T Cell Function
content:
Self‐propelled antigen‐presenting microrobots mechanically stimulate T cells through dynamic immune synapses, driving mechanotransduction‐dependent metabolic fitness and stem‐like programming. This motion‐enabled strategy enhances CAR‐T cell expansion, persistence, and antitumor efficacy, highlighting microrobotic antigen‐presenting interfaces as a new platform for cell therapy engineering.








ABSTRACT
Mechanical forces are emerging as key regulators of T‐cell function, yet how active motion‐ derived mechanical cues from artificial antigen‐presenting cells (aAPCs) influence T‐cell activation and fate remains largely unexplored. Here, we develop self‐propelled antigen‐presenting microrobots (CytoBots)—gas‐driven magnesium microparticles functionalized with anti‐CD3 and anti‐CD28 antibodies—that actively navigate suspension environments and mechanically engage T cells. Unlike immotile aAPCs, CytoBots generate motion‐dependent, force‐bearing stimulation that enhances T‐cell activation. Single‐cell force spectroscopy shows that CytoBots double receptor–ligand binding strength and extend bond lifetime threefold, supporting a role for motion‐enhanced mechanical interactions in T‐cell activation. CytoBot stimulation is associated with enhanced proximal T‐cell signaling, increased phosphorylation of AKT and mTOR, and metabolic changes characterized by elevated mitochondrial respiration and glycolysis‐associated activity. These responses accompany the enrichment of stem‐like and central memory T‐cell populations. In humanized tumor models, CytoBot‐expanded CAR‐T cells exhibit superior cytotoxicity, persistence, and antitumor efficacy. These findings establish microrobotic antigen‐presenting interfaces as a generalizable strategy for programming immune cell function through dynamic mechanotransduction, opening new opportunities for next‐generation cell therapies.

title: Interface Engineering to Unlock Multi‐Electron Sn+/S2− Redox Reaction and High Lithium Anode Utilization
content:
The inherent difference in migration kinetics between chloride and iodide ions drives spontaneous halogen‐mediated phase separation at the electrode/electrolyte interface, which enables all‐solid‐state battery to achieve excellent electrochemical performance.








ABSTRACT
All‐solid‐state lithium–sulfur batteries (ASSLSBs) offer high theoretical energy density, yet their practical viability is impeded by sluggish cathodic redox kinetics and uncontrolled anodic dendrite growth. Here, we address these challenges by a dual‐interface engineering strategy that exploits halogen anion migration to in situ construct phase‐separated localized electrochemical microreactors (LEMRs) at both electrodes. At the cathode, an in situ‐formed Li6PS5Cl/LiCl/Li2S‐LiI internal LEMR activates the S2−/Sn+ (n ≥1) multi‐electron redox reaction beyond the conventional S2−/S0 redox reaction while maintaining structural integrity. Concurrently, at the Li anode, an interfacial LiCl/C@LiI/LiCl‐LiI anode LEMR confines Li plating/stripping within the LEMR to suppress lithium dendrites. This dual‐LEMR architecture enables the optimized cells to deliver a capacity retention of 86.3% after 450 cycles at 3.6 mAh cm−2 and 80% after 70 cycles at a high areal capacity of 7.5 mAh cm−2 under a low N/P ratio of 0.78, and to achieve an ultra‐high areal capacity of 32.8 mAh cm−2. This work highlights the potential of anion chemistry as an effective interface engineering strategy to overcome the kinetics and stability limits of all‐solid‐state lithium batteries, and provides a versatile framework for advancing high‐energy ASSLSBs.

title: Synergistic Water‐Deficient Inner Helmholtz Plane and Asymmetric Dual‐Site Nonmetal Catalysts Enable Stable Ah‐Level Aqueous Zn–I2 Batteries at Elevated Temperatures
content:
At the anode, a marginally hydrophilic and conductive modification layer with a hexagonal layered structure is constructed to suppress hydrogen evolution and promote (002)‐oriented electrodeposits. At the cathode, asymmetric dual‐site nonmetal single‐atom–cluster structures are designed to enhance iodine adsorption and accelerate conversion kinetics. This synergistic approach enables stable Ah‐level aqueous Zn–I2 batteries at elevated temperatures.








ABSTRACT
At elevated temperatures, intensified water‐induced side reactions and iodine dissolution severely hinder the development of aqueous zinc–iodine batteries. Herein, a marginally hydrophilic and conductive modification layer with a hexagonal layered structure is constructed to stabilize the anode interface. This approach establishes a water‐deficient inner Helmholtz plane and reduces the fraction of weak hydrogen bonds, thereby suppressing spontaneous Zn dissolution and water decomposition. Concurrently, interfacial electronic structure regulation increases the energy barrier for the hydrogen evolution reaction and promotes uniform Zn deposition along the Zn‐(002) crystal plane, effectively inhibiting dendrite growth. These effects are corroborated by theoretical calculations and in situ characterizations. Furthermore, asymmetric dual‐site nonmetal single‐atom–cluster structures are introduced into the cathode host to enhance iodine adsorption and accelerate conversion kinetics, thereby mitigating iodine dissolution. Benefiting from this synergistic design, the assembled coin‐type battery delivers a discharge capacity of 95 mAh g−1 after 60 000 cycles at 8 A g−1. A sub‐ampere‐hour‐level plastic‐cased battery employing a high‐loading cathode with a theoretical areal‐capacity of 5.6 mAh cm−2 further demonstrates strong practical potential by maintaining excellent cycling stability at 3 C and at 50°C. An Ah‐level pouch battery also exhibits stable operation at 50°C.

title: Covalent–Ionic Bonding Regulation Enables Chemo‐Mechanical Stabilization of High‐Voltage O3‐Type Sodium Layered Oxide Cathodes
content:
Guided by hard and soft acids and bases (HSAB) theory, a covalent–ionic bonding regulation strategy is developed to decouple chemo‐mechanical degradation in high‐voltage O3‐type sodium layered oxide cathodes. The covalent Ti─O framework suppresses structural degradation, while the localized Mg─F ionic coordination stabilizes lattice oxygen, enabling highly reversible high‐voltage electrochemistry.








ABSTRACT
Ni–Fe–Mn‐based O3‐type layered oxides are attractive cathode materials for sodium‐ion batteries, but their high‐voltage operation suffers from the coupling between phase transitions and lattice oxygen instability. In this work, guided by hard and soft acids and bases (HSAB) theory, we propose a covalent–ionic dual‐pathway decoupling strategy to stabilize high‐voltage O3‐type layered cathodes. The incorporation of Mg, Ti, and F constructs a rigid architecture in which a covalent Ti─O framework reinforces the transition‐metal octahedral skeleton to suppress detrimental phase transitions, while localized Mg─F ionic coordination stabilizes lattice oxygen through localized electrostatic anchoring to mitigate irreversible oxygen release. Through multiscale structural and spectroscopic analyses, we verify that this bonding regulation suppresses the O3→P3→OP2 multiphase evolution and lattice oxygen escape. The modified cathode maintains 76.32% capacity retention over 400 cycles at 1 C and exhibits robust cyclability across −10°C to 50°C; the assembled full cells achieve a reversible capacity of 166.27 mAh g−1 with an energy density of 330.22 Wh kg−1 at 0.1 C, and an initial capacity of 143.74 mAh g−1 with 72.06% retention after 500 cycles at 1 C. This work demonstrates a bonding‐regulation paradigm that decouples chemo‐mechanical degradation in high‐energy‐density layered oxide cathodes.

title: Pulse‐Programmable Electrostatic Memory Using Ultrathin Hexagonal Boron Nitride
content:
Upper panel: Schematic illustration of the device geometry, showing the underlying channel material encapsulated by a thin inserted hBN, with all metal electrodes fabricated on top of the hBN. Lower panel: Hysteretic memory response of the device, showing the evolution of the read resistance (Rread) under a staircase sequence of write‐current pulses (Iwrite), with State‐1 and State‐2 indicated.








ABSTRACT
Non‐volatile memory elements that enable multifunctionality and seamless integration with emerging quantum materials are of increasing interest for next‐generation electronic systems. In van der Waals heterostructures, hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is widely employed as an inert substrate, encapsulation layer, and gate dielectric. Here we show that ultrathin (∼1.2 nm) hBN can also function as an active, pulse‐programmable electrostatic medium, enabling non‐volatile resistive memory with tunable resistance states in a multi‐terminal device architecture without dedicated gate or floating‐gate elements. Under millisecond current pulses, devices exhibit robust polarity‐dependent hysteresis in both transverse and longitudinal resistance, with programmed states exhibiting long retention times up to room temperature. The switching amplitude is strongly enhanced near the charge‐neutrality regime and vanishes in control devices without hBN, establishing ultrathin hBN as the essential functional element. We attribute this behavior to field‐assisted charge injection and trapping in hBN and near its interfaces, generating metastable electret‐like states that modify the local electrostatic potential landscape and thereby reconfigure electronic transport in the underlying channel. Our results identify few‐layer hBN as an active dielectric platform for non‐volatile memory and reveal a route toward electrostatically programmable transport functionalities in van der Waals systems.

title: Hole Mobility Synchronizes Carbon Oxidation and Nitrate Reduction to Switch Photocatalytic Selectivity between Ammonia and Urea
content:
Hole mobility functions as a kinetic master switch for selective nitrate photoreduction. Introducing Cd‐vacancy (VCd) into single‐atom Cu‐anchored CdS enhances hole mobility, enabling oxidative C–C cleavage of oxalic acid (OA) to generate *COOH for orientated coupling with nitrate‐derived *NH2 at electron‐localized Cu to afford urea. In contrast, vacancy‐free CdS with low hole mobility drives deep nitrate protonation to ammonia.








ABSTRACT
Photocatalytic conversion of nitrate and renewable carbon feedstocks offers a sustainable route to nitrogen chemicals but remains constrained by mismatched oxidation–reduction kinetics and inefficient C–N coupling. Here, we identify hole mobility as a decisive kinetic regulator that governs nitrate photoreduction selectivity by synchronizing carbon activation and nitrogen reduction pathways. By introducing cadmium vacancies into single‐atom Cu‐anchored CdS, we substantially reduce effective hole mass and accelerate hole transport, enabling oxidative C–C cleavage of biomass‐derived oxalic‐acid to generate reactive *COOH. Concurrently, hole mobility‐induced electron localization at Cu stabilizes nitrate‐derived *NH2, promoting selective *NH2‐*COOH coupling while suppressing deep protonation to ammonia. Accordingly, Cu/CdS‐VCd achieves a record urea yield of 1024 µmol g−1 h−1 with >99% selectivity, approximately fourteen times higher than state‐of‐the‐art nitrate‐based photocatalysts. In contrast, vacancy‐free Cu/CdS with low hole mobility fails to activate carbon feedstock and instead produces ammonia with >99% selectivity. In‐situ spectroscopy and density functional theory reveal that enhanced hole mobility accelerates oxalic‐acid oxidation, strengthens *NH2 adsorption, and lowers the free‐energy barrier for C–N coupling to enable selective urea formation. These findings establish charge‐carrier mobility, rather than isolated active‐site activity, as a governing principle for artificial photosynthesis, offering a general strategy for selective multi‐reactant photocatalytic transformations.

title: Novel Fluorinated Amino‐Ester Electrolyte With Host–Guest Solvation Enables High‐Voltage and Thermally Safe Lithium–Metal Batteries
content:
This work reports a molecular fluorination strategy for synthesizing two previously unexplored amide solvents, N,N‐dimethylcarbamate trifluoroethyl (TFE) and N,N‐dimethylcarbamate hexafluoroisopropyl (HFS), which form a host–guest type solvation structure due to their differing degrees of fluorination. This structure not only enhances lithium‐ion transport kinetics but also improves interfacial stability, ultimately achieving significant overall performance enhancement in high‐voltage lithium–metal batteries.








ABSTRACT
Lithium–metal batteries (LMBs) face critical bottlenecks to high energy density, long cycle life, and thermal safety, mainly due to insufficient oxidation stability and thermal tolerance of solvation structures in conventional carbonate/ether electrolytes. In this work, we develop a host–guest solvation structure via a molecular fluorination strategy based on a tertiary amine‐ester scaffold functionalized with trifluoroethyl (CF3CH2─) and hexafluoroisopropyl ((CF3)2CH─) groups, affording two fluorinated solvents: N, N‐dimethylcarbamate trifluoroethyl (TFE) and N,N‐dimethylcarbamate hexafluoroisopropyl (HFS). The distinct polarity contrast between TFE and HFS delivers functional complementarity: TFE, with strong Lewis basicity, promotes lithium‐salt dissociation, while highly fluorinated HFS, with weak solvation ability, accelerates interfacial reduction kinetics through a delocalized charge‐transfer mechanism, forming a LiF/Li2O‐rich nanocrystalline solid electrolyte interphase. Consequently, in Li||LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 configurations, the as‐designed electrolyte enables a 10 Ah pouch cell to stably cycle over 260 cycles with 95.2% capacity retention, and a 4.5 V‐charged 22.4 Ah pouch cell delivers an initial energy density of 550 Wh kg−1. The pouch cell also survives nail penetration and exhibits significantly delayed thermal runaway. This amino‐ester molecular design offers key insights for developing high‐energy, safe LMBs toward practical industrial applications.

title: Food‐Interfaced Bioelectronics for In Situ Molecular Food Profiling
content:
This review highlights recent advances in food‐interfaced bioelectronics for monitoring food composition, quality, freshness, and safety. It discusses key developments in food‐compatible materials, molecular recognition, signal transduction, sampling and device integration, together with emerging data‐driven and wireless technologies. By connecting fundamental sensing principles with practical challenges in real‐food environments, this review provides perspectives on the translation of food‐interfaced bioelectronics toward intelligent, decentralized, and sustainable food systems.








ABSTRACT
Over the past decade, real‐time sensing technologies have assumed an increasingly important role in monitoring food taste, quality, and safety by probing diverse biomolecular signatures within complex food matrices. Distinct from conventional food sensors, emerging food‐interfaced bioelectronic platforms combine advances in materials science, molecular recognition, and device engineering to enable direct and in situ access to food‐relevant information. Recent efforts have increasingly focused on sustainable, biocompatible, and, in some cases, edible materials that can safely interface with foods while maintaining robust performance in chemically and mechanically heterogeneous environments. Coupled with unobtrusive, multimodal sensing platforms and data‐driven analytical frameworks, these systems offer new opportunities for real‐time food profiling, informed consumption, and waste reduction. This review surveys recent progress in food‐interfaced sensing technologies, with particular emphasis on materials innovations, interface design considerations, sensing and signal transduction strategies, and application‐driven data interpretation. We further discuss the key translational challenges associated with validation, scalability, and regulatory adoption. By bridging materials, devices, and food systems, food‐interfaced bioelectronics have the potential to transform food monitoring, food safety, and personalized nutrition.

title: Hypoxia‐Regulating Nanozymes for Biomedicine
content:
Hypoxia caused by an imbalance between oxygen supply and consumption contributes to numerous pathological conditions, including cardiovascular diseases, tumors, inflammation, and fibrosis. Nanozymes act as multifunctional enzyme mimics with tunable catalytic properties that regulate oxidative stress, metabolism, and immunity in the hypoxic microenvironment. This review highlights how nanozyme systems provide innovative approaches for the precise treatment of hypoxia‐associated diseases.








ABSTRACT
Hypoxic microenvironments arise when local oxygen supply fails to meet cellular demand and exert an influence on the progression of cancer, ischemic heart and brain injury, chronic inflammatory disorders, and other diseases. Conventional approaches, including oxygen delivery systems, small‐molecule redox drugs, and natural enzymes, can relieve hypoxia but suffer from poor tissue specificity, short duration of action, and limited stability. Nanozymes are engineered nanomaterials with enzyme‐like catalytic activity. Through controllable redox reactions, they can regulate oxygen generation or consumption, rebalance reactive oxygen species, and reprogram hypoxic microenvironments at the cellular and tissue levels. In recent years, the field has shifted from empirical trial‐and‐error to rational nanozyme design, with a focus on defined active sites, disease‐responsive activity, and targeted delivery. Herein, we summarize the key design principles governing nanozyme catalytic performance and discuss the catalytic mechanisms involved in hypoxia regulation. We then examine how distinct pathological features of acute and chronic hypoxic microenvironments create different catalytic requirements and how nanozyme functions can be tailored accordingly. Furthermore, we provide an overview of nanozyme applications across hypoxia‐associated diseases and discuss emerging opportunities and barriers for clinical translation. This review is expected to provide insights for developing precise and clinically valuable hypoxia‐regulating nanozymes.

title: Construction and Regulation of Defect Electrocatalysts for Rechargeable Li–O2 Batteries
content:
Defect engineering reconstructs oxygen reaction pathways and interfacial reaction mechanisms in Li–O2 batteries (LOBs) by tailoring active sites and electronic structures. This review systematically summarizes the construction strategies, structure–activity relationships, and catalytic mechanisms of defect‐engineered catalysts, and highlights future directions toward emerging reaction chemistries and highly reversible LOBs.








ABSTRACT
Li–O2 batteries (LOBs) have garnered significant interest due to their extraordinarily high theoretical energy density. Nonetheless, their development is severely constrained by sluggish kinetics at the cathodic three‐phase interfaces. Addressing these limitations hinges on the rational design of electrocatalysts capable of efficiently promoting both the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Central to catalytic performance is the precise modulation of electronic structure, particularly the creation of nonuniform surface charge distributions to expose highly active sites and optimize the adsorption energy of key intermediates. Among various strategies, defect engineering has emerged as a powerful approach for tailoring surface electronic properties. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in defect‐engineered cathode materials for nonaqueous LOBs. The characteristic defect types and their influences on oxygen electrocatalysis are analyzed, followed by an in‐depth discussion of the fundamental roles of defects in electronic structure modulation, interfacial synergistic catalysis, and catalyst stability. By correlating defect configurations with electrochemical performance, this review aims to establish clear structure–activity–performance relationships for rational catalyst design. Finally, future opportunities involving promising catalyst systems, advanced defect design strategies, integrated catalytic systems, and remaining challenges for defect electrocatalysts are outlined to promote the practical implementation of LOB technologies.

title: From Phosphor Ceramics to Intelligent Light‐Conversion Materials: High‐Flux Luminescence, Glassy Composite Interface, and Machine‐Learning‐Guided Design
content:
Phosphor ceramics are emerging as robust light‐conversion platforms for next‐generation high‐power LED/LD lighting, laser display, and near‐infrared sources. This review highlights how luminescent centers, ceramic microstructures, scattering, thermal transport, glassy interfaces, and data‐driven design can be integrated to achieve high‐flux emission, improved stability, and reliable device performance under demanding operating conditions.








ABSTRACT
High‐power LED/LD and NIR applications demand phosphors that remain efficient and stable under high‐flux excitation, whereas conventional phosphor/organic systems are limited by heat buildup, interfacial degradation, and luminescence saturation. Phosphor ceramics provide a robust all‐inorganic alternative, but their photothermal coupling mechanisms and cross‐scale design principles remain insufficiently summarized. Here, we review recent advances in phosphor ceramics with a particular focus on photothermal coupling in high‐flux light conversion. We establish a composition‐structure‐photothermal behavior‐device performance framework that connects activator ions, host chemistry, defects and grain boundaries with light absorption, scattering regulation, thermal‐transport pathways, and device‐level output. Recent advances in garnet‐based, multiphase, multicolor visible, and NIR phosphor ceramics are discussed, with emphasis on compositional regulation, ceramic processing, microstructure engineering, and LED/LD integration. We clarify key relationships among transparency, absorption efficiency, scattering strength, thermal conductivity, interfacial thermal resistance, and luminescence saturation thresholds, which collectively determine high‐brightness reliability under extreme photon and heat loads. Emerging glassy composite interfaces are further highlighted for low‐temperature integration, heterogeneous packaging, and multimaterial coupling. Finally, we discuss machine learning as an enabling tool for candidate screening, processing‐window optimization, property prediction, and multi‐objective device design, offering guidance for next‐generation stable, intelligent light‐conversion materials.

title: Modular Bio‐Integrated Materials and Devices for Advanced Theranostic Healthcare
content:
Modular bio‐integrated theranostic systems (MBTS) integrate sensing, analysis, interaction, and therapy to enable continuous monitoring, feedback‐guided decisions, and on‐demand intervention. This review establishes a modular framework spanning wearable and implantable bio‐interfaces, compares open‐loop, semi‐closed‐loop, and fully autonomous closed‐loop architectures, highlights representative healthcare applications, and examines key barriers to reliable, scalable, and clinically translatable personalized healthcare.








ABSTRACT
Bio‐integrated theranostic systems that combine sensing, analysis, interaction, and therapy are emerging as powerful platforms for personalized healthcare. Unlike conventional diagnostic or therapeutic devices, modular bio‐integrated systems integrate body‐conformal or implantable interfaces with analytical units, user‐interaction platforms, and therapeutic modules to enable continuous monitoring, feedback‐guided decision‐making, and on‐demand intervention. In this review, we summarize progress in modular bio‐integrated theranostic systems (MBTS) from four functional perspectives. First, we discuss biophysical, biochemical, and multimodal sensing modules that provide physiological and molecular inputs across skin‐interfaced, wound‐integrated, ocular, oral, and implantable formats. We review analysis modules that convert sensor‐derived signals into health‐state assessments, risk estimates, and intervention guidance. Interactive interfaces and feedback modules are discussed, focusing on visual and graphical interfaces for data presentation and interactive feedback for user engagement and therapeutic response. Finally, programmable therapeutic modules for controlled drug delivery and nonpharmacological intervention are summarized, followed by biomedical implementations in drug delivery, neuromodulation, diabetes management, wound care, blood pressure regulation, and other healthcare scenarios. We further discuss engineering challenges related to module integration, bio‐interface stability, power supply, data security, and cost‐effective manufacturing. This review provides a modular framework for designing next‐generation bio‐integrated theranostic systems that connect sensing, analysis, interaction, and therapy within healthcare platforms.

title: Architecting Mesoporous Heterojunctions via Programmable Interfacial Engineering
content:
Mesoporosity transforms hetero‐phase contact into functionally accessible junctions by opening transport pathways, stabilizing interfacial nanodomains, and integrating confined reaction spaces with interfacial electronic polarization. This study establishes effective heterojunctions as a unifying framework, maps MHJ configurations and construction strategies onto the interfacial engineering across specific application contexts, and highlights AI‐guided, quantitative, operando, and scalable directions toward programmable interface design.








ABSTRACT
Mesoporous heterojunction materials (MHJs), integrating interconnected mesopore networks with electronically polarized heterointerfaces, have delivered unparalleled advantages across diverse frontier fields. Open mesopores expose otherwise buried junctions, shorten diffusion pathways, and create confined nanospaces, while heterointerfaces generate built‐in electric fields and interfacial barriers that steer carrier migration and reaction trajectories. Despite substantial advances in mesoporous materials and heterostructures, the mesopore‐enabled amplification of heterojunction functions has not been systematically articulated. This Review reframes MHJs through the concept of effective heterojunctions, emphasizing active interface accessibility and local electronic perturbation validity as central design criteria. The mechanistic roles of mesoporosity in interfacial barrier modulation, charge utilization, and microenvironment regulation are delineated, and their manifestations across representative MHJ configurations, synthetic strategies, and applications are systematically examined. Key challenges and opportunities are also outlined in artificial intelligence (AI)‐guided predictive design, effective junction quantification, operando characterization, and scalable synthesis. This Review aims to establish a clearer guiding principle to promote MHJs progression from experience‐based material integration toward precise interface programming.

title: Nanoscale Thermocatalysis: Mechanisms, Regulation, and Biomedical Applications
content:
This review highlights thermal‐driven catalysis as an active energy‐conversion paradigm, moving beyond heat as a mere byproduct. It establishes the fundamental roles of nanoscale heat transport, non‐Fourier effects, and material engineering—defects, heterojunctions, phases, and interfaces—in steering thermoelectric, pyroelectric, and thermo‐enhanced processes. These principles underpin emerging biomedical strategies, from antibacterial and antitumor therapies to self‐powered biosensing and tissue regeneration.








ABSTRACT
Thermal‐driven catalysis has emerged as a promising interdisciplinary field that integrates thermal science, catalysis, nanotechnology, and biomedicine by utilizing thermal energy as a driving force for catalytic reactions. Unlike conventional catalytic systems, thermal‐driven catalysis exploits temperature gradients, thermal fluctuations, or localized heating to induce charge separation, accelerate reaction kinetics, and regulate interfacial redox processes. This review systematically summarizes the fundamental mechanisms of thermoelectric catalysis, pyroelectric catalysis, and thermo‐enhanced catalytic reactions, with particular emphasis on the role of nanoscale heat transport and non‐Fourier thermal behavior in thermal energy conversion. Recent advances in material engineering strategies, including defect engineering, heterojunction engineering, phase engineering, morphology engineering, interface engineering, and emerging approaches such as entropy, spin, and single‐atom engineering, are comprehensively discussed. Furthermore, representative biomedical applications, including photothermal and plasmonic nanomedicine, pyroelectric catalysis, thermoelectric catalysis, and thermally regulated catalytic systems, are highlighted in the contexts of antibacterial therapy, tumor treatment, biosensing, and tissue engineering. Finally, current challenges and future perspectives regarding material design, energy‐conversion efficiency, mechanistic understanding, and clinical translation are discussed. This review provides a comprehensive overview of thermal‐driven catalysis and offers insights into the development of next‐generation catalytic platforms for advanced biomedical applications.
